newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Budapest, Bucharest mkts in record-breaking form.
newsitem.headline: Budapest, Bucharest mkts in record-breaking form.

text.p: Budapest and Bucharest outperformed other central European markets this week as they hit record highs on the back of fresh capital.
Prague also firmed although political uncertainties remained. Ljubljana, Warsaw, Bratislava eased while Zageb was mixed.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements in 72 Czech, Hungarian, Polish, Slovak and Slovenian shares, edged up.
BUDAPEST
The Budapest bourse on Thursday ended at a fifth successive record high but the overall picture suggested that a phase of calmer trading was imminent as the holiday season approached.

"The market is in a danger of drifting sideways but I think it is going to be a problem not just for Hungary but maybe for several markets as well," said Nigel Rendell, emerging market strategist at HSBC James Capel in London.
The bourse soared until Wednesday on a strong dollar and on fresh money flowing in from the Czech market as well as from U.S. mutual funds which were said to be appearing as new players.
But from Wednesday arbitrage between the cash and futures markets and profit-taking appeared to trim some of earlier gains.
BUCHAREST
Most Bucharest stocks drifted higher early this week as sellers waiting for higher prices thinned supply.

On Thursday prices touched new highs on rising volumes as foreign investors enhanced their presence in the market after the government approved portfolio investment rules, setting a capital gains repatriation tax of four percent.
The unofficial VAB index computed by market capitalisation and average prices rose by 24 percent from Wednesday. The other independent index, the BIG, was unavailable. PRAGUE

A return of foreign investors pushed Czech share prices higher for most of the week before renewed political uncertainty forced most on to the sidelines. The Prague bourse's PX50 index ended on Thursday at 4,976, up 90 on the week.
Dealers said interest in several blue chips had given rise to a wave of optimism that prices had fallen to levels that made them too attractive to pass up.
But a confidence vote called for next Tuesday coupled with infighting among the governing coalition squelched what little momentum the market had gained.

"It looks like many investors are going to wait to see the result of the confidence vote and then, based on that, they will either take or not take positions," said Lubos Vystavel, a trader at ING Barings in Prague.
WARSAW
Polish shares fell this week on large sales on the primary market but analysts expected a rebound at least at the beginning of the next week in reaction to the falls.

But they said the upside was limited as the primary market was drawing investor capital and attention to offers such as those of Bank Handlowy in which one billion zlotys' worth of shares are on sale and copper giant KGHM expected in June.
"The market might rise in the beginning of the week but later there might be falls on profit-taking," said Grzegorz Cimochowski, an analyst at ING Barings.
Analysts said that in the longer-term the market might keep its sideways drift until elections expected in September.
BRATISLAVA
Trading on the Bratislava Stock Exchange was quiet throughout the week with dealers anticipating little change until the liquidity squeeze on the interbank market eases off.
"I don't expect this situation to improve unless some liquidity appears in the system," Peter Krutil of Creditanstalt Securities said.

The Slovak central bank has been keeping the interbank market short of liquidity as a means to protecting the crown. However equities dealers say this has had the knock-on effect of choking off funds for dealing in shares.
LJUBLJANA

Slovenian shares eased 0.56 percent this week to 1,315.96 points on Thursday and traders said a falling trend was likely to continue over the summer as no fresh foreign money or information that could boost prices was expected.

Market participants said future movements on the market would largely depend on ratification of the EU association accord signed June 1996 as it would attract international investors to resume their activity.

"I am afraid foreign players are already losing their patience and according to my information some of them are already switching to neighbouring markets that are apparently more attractive," said Jasna Zontar, trader at brokerage Modra.

On Thursday the Constitutional Court said parliament could not ratify the EU accord because it was in contradiction to the constitutional article that prohibits foreigners to own land in Slovenia, thus delaying the ratification.
ZAGREB

Croatian stocks closed mixed in lively trade on Thursday as market activity picked up steadily throughout the week and traders said renewed interest from foreign investors was likely to push prices upward.
